params.text:
Why fire safety matters in care

Fire is one of the most serious risks in any care setting. The people you support are often the most vulnerable in a fire: they may have limited mobility, sensory impairments, dementia or medical conditions that mean they cannot recognise danger or escape without help. A fire that a healthy adult could walk away from can be fatal for a resident who relies on you.

This module explains how fires start, how to prevent them, how to respond if one breaks out, and how people are safely evacuated in a care home or a person's own home. Fire safety is everyone's responsibility, not just the manager's or the fire marshal's.

By the end of this course you should be able to:

  • Explain the law that governs fire safety and who the "responsible person" is.
  • Describe the fire triangle and the common causes of fire in care.
  • Take practical steps to prevent fires, including reducing the risk from emollient creams.
  • Raise the alarm correctly and support a safe evacuation.

The law: the Fire Safety Order 2005

Fire safety in workplaces and care premises in England and Wales is governed by the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, usually shortened to the Fire Safety Order. It applies to almost every care setting — care homes, supported living and the offices behind a home care service — and covers the safety of everyone who could be affected, including the people you support, visitors and staff.

The Order places most legal duties on a "responsible person" — usually the care home owner, provider, employer or registered manager. Where more than one person has some control of a building, they must co-operate so that fire safety is never left to chance.

Fire risk assessments and your duties

The responsible person must make sure a suitable and sufficient fire risk assessment is carried out, keep it up to date (normally reviewed at least once a year), and act on what it finds. The assessment identifies the fire hazards on the premises, decides who is at risk, and sets out the measures needed to keep everyone safe — including alarms, fire doors, emergency lighting, evacuation plans and staff training. In a care home it must take account of residents who cannot self-evacuate, especially at night when staffing is lower.

Although the legal duties sit with the responsible person, every worker has a part to play:

  • Follow the findings: work in line with the fire procedures the assessment leads to.
  • Co-operate: take part in the training and fire drills your employer arranges.
  • Do not add risk: avoid anything that creates a fire hazard or blocks an escape route.
  • Report concerns: tell your employer about faults, missing signs or blocked exits straight away.

Failure to comply with the Order can lead to enforcement notices, heavy fines or prosecution.

params.question: Under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, fire safety is only the manager's concern and frontline care staff have no responsibilities.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. Although the law names a "responsible person" with overall duties, keeping people safe depends on every member of staff playing their part every day.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The "responsible person" has overall legal duties, but fire safety relies on every worker – spotting hazards, keeping fire doors shut, knowing the evacuation plan and raising the alarm.

params.question: Under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, whose legal duty is it to make sure a fire risk assessment is carried out and kept up to date?

answers.text: The ‘responsible person’, usually the employer, owner or registered manager.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Order places this duty on the responsible person, who must arrange the assessment and act on its findings.

answers.text: Each individual care worker, for the rooms they work in.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. You must co-operate and report concerns, but arranging the assessment is the responsible person’s duty, not yours.
Incorrect. The fire service enforces the law and may inspect, but the duty to assess and manage the risk sits with the responsible person.
Incorrect. The people you support are those the assessment protects; the legal duty rests with the responsible person.
